claims.text: The composition of the native oxide layer on pre-exposure Q235 steel controls the onset of localized corrosion.
The continuity of the native oxide layer on pre-exposure Q235 steel controls the onset of localized corrosion.
Increasing temperature from approximately 25 °C to 70–80 °C accelerates diffusion relevant to oxide-film formation or repair on Q235 steel.
Accelerated diffusion at 70–80 °C repairs or forms a more continuous protective oxide film on Q235 steel.
A more uniform and continuous oxide film acts as a barrier against aggressive species.
Slower oxide-response kinetics at 25 °C produce incomplete or nonuniform oxide coverage on Q235 steel.
Incomplete or nonuniform oxide coverage increases localized corrosion initiation on Q235 steel.
As-received Q235 steel has inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
As-received Q235 steel has a native, non-optimized oxide layer.
Relative to samples at 25 °C, Q235 samples exposed at 70–80 °C will have lower corrosion current density.
Relative to samples at 25 °C, Q235 samples exposed at 70–80 °C will have higher electrochemical impedance.
Relative to samples at 25 °C, Q235 samples exposed at 70–80 °C will have a denser and more uniform oxide film.
Relative to samples at 70–80 °C, Q235 samples exposed at 25 °C will display more localized corrosion features.
Electrochemical impedance behavior can provide evidence for the presence of a passivation layer.
Variations in initial microstructure or oxide composition may change the magnitude of the proposed protective effect.
Temperature-dependent changes in oxide chemical stability may compete with the proposed protective effect.
